newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SIMEX fuel oil market struggles after relaunch.
newsitem.headline: SIMEX fuel oil market struggles after relaunch.

text.p: Singapore's "new-look" fuel oil futures contract is failing to win much more industry interest than its ill-fated predecessor in its first month of trading.
The Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) had hoped it could revive fuel oil futures trading with new specifications and relaunched the contract on April 22.
But one month later, average daily turnover is just 57 lots, or 5,700 tonnes, and few oil players said they planned to participate in the market in the near term.
"There is not enough liquidity in the market to inspire trading," said one trader with a major oil company, adding that he would not enter the market until liquidity improved.
By late Thursday, no transactions were reported on SIMEX after several hours of trade. Just eight lots were traded on Tuesday.
On April 22 there were 325 lots traded, the biggest trading day so far since the relaunch.
Traders said SIMEX offered a regulated market that was not so easy to manipulate.
Most traders also preferred to use fuel oil swaps -- an over-the-counter derivative -- which have a monthly turnover of more than 1.5 million tonnes.
"It's not a problem of specifications. It's mainly a psychological problem," said a source familiar with the market.
"If you don't take part, liquidity will not increase and fewer people will join and there will be even less liquidity," the source said.

The fuel oil contract was first listed on SIMEX in 1989 and traded 5,000 contracts per day. But the market fell dormant in late 1995 because the specifications were out of line with the underlying physical market.
The contract briefly traded again for a few days in October last year.
In April, SIMEX revised the specifications of the contract, to bring it more into line with the physical market.
SIMEX officials said they had hoped the revised contract would become an additional option for traders to hedge their risk on the existing over-the-counter swaps market.
"Theoretically, it's good to have a regulated market to hedge your risk, but the SIMEX mechanism is different from that at the cargo and swaps markets," said one trader.
"At the end of the day, you don't want to work on several different mechanisms to calculate your risk," the trader said.
"It's easier and cheaper to take part in the swaps market, with fewer restrictions, why bother to be in the SIMEX market?" said one supplier of bunker fuels for shipping.
"To be honest, I don't think SIMEX can take away business from the paper market, which most people have been used to for a long, long time," he said.
